title: AI vs voicemail for restaurant phone calls
seoTitle: AI vs voicemail for restaurant owners | ROAL
description: Compare AI and voicemail for restaurant calls, see where each falls short, and find a simple setup for busy phones and after-hours calls.
question: Should my restaurant use an AI phone host or voicemail?
answer: For most restaurants, an AI phone host is better than voicemail because it can answer common questions, take pickup and delivery orders, and send the order to the kitchen screen right away. Voicemail only records a message, so the caller still has to wait for a callback and you still have to listen, write, and re-enter the order later.
summary: You’ll be able to compare voicemail and an AI phone host, then set up the phone flow that fits your restaurant.
intro:
AI vs voicemail for a restaurant is really a choice between collecting the order now or asking the caller to leave a message. Voicemail is cheaper to set up, but it usually creates more work later and can cost sales when people hang up.

An AI phone host answers the phone, takes the order, quotes a ready time, and passes clean tickets to the kitchen. ROAL does that for restaurants, and you can test it from your website or menu before going live. See [how it works](/how-it-works) if you want the setup flow first.

sections.h2: What happens to a call when you use voicemail instead?
sections.body:
Voicemail sounds simple, but for a restaurant it usually pushes the work to later. The caller hears a greeting, leaves a message, and waits for someone to call back. If it is rush hour, the message may sit until the line slows down, and by then the caller may have already ordered somewhere else.

That delay matters for real restaurant tasks. A pizza shop caller might want a large pepperoni, extra cheese, and no onions. With voicemail, you still have to listen to the message, figure out the order, check the menu, call back, confirm details, and then get it into the kitchen. With an AI phone host, the order is collected during the call and sent to the kitchen screen as a clean ticket.

A simple voicemail script looks like this:
- "Please leave your name, number, and order, and we’ll call you back as soon as we can."

A phone host script can sound more like:
- "What size would you like, and do you want any toppings?"

sections.h2: When does voicemail still make sense for a restaurant?
sections.body:
Voicemail still has a place, but usually as a backup, not the main plan. It can help after hours, during staff shortages, or for calls that need a person to review them later. Some owners also like voicemail for rare situations that need manual follow-up, like a complicated complaint or a request outside the normal menu.

A practical setup is to let the restaurant ring normally first, then forward unanswered calls to voicemail or to an AI phone host. If you want to compare the tradeoffs, [AI phone host vs voicemail](/compare/voicemail) is the cleanest place to start. The key is not to let every call end in a message box when your menu is actually orderable.

Use this checklist:
- Keep voicemail greeting short.
- Tell callers when to expect a callback.
- Use it only for overflow or after-hours fallback.
- Make sure the voicemail inbox is checked often.
- Do not rely on voicemail for busy meal periods if you want pickup orders to keep moving.

sections.h2: What does an AI phone host do better than voicemail?
sections.body:
An AI phone host can handle the kind of calls restaurants get all day: hours, address, parking, menu questions, pickup orders, delivery orders, reservation requests, and even multilingual callers. ROAL also leaves sold-out items off the call flow, so callers are not ordering something the kitchen cannot make.

Here is what that changes at the counter and in the kitchen:
| Call type | Voicemail | AI phone host |
|---|---|---|
| Hours or address question | Caller leaves a message | Answers right away |
| Pickup order | Message to decode later | Takes the order live |
| Allergy-sensitive request | Easy to miss | Hands off to staff with a summary |
| Manager complaint | Delayed follow-up | Routes to staff with context |

A useful script line is: "Your order will be ready around 20 minutes." The host can say that only after collecting the items, sizes, modifiers, and notes. That is a better restaurant experience than asking people to leave a message and hope someone gets back to them.

sections.h2: How much work does voicemail create compared with pay-per-order pricing?
sections.body:
Voicemail itself may not have a big monthly fee, but it can create hidden labor. Someone has to listen, interpret, call back, repeat questions, and enter the order again. If you are paying staff to do that work, the real cost is not zero.

Here is a simple example you can swap for your own numbers. Say you get 10 voicemail orders in a day, and each one takes 5 minutes to listen to, call back, confirm, and key in. That is 50 minutes a day. If you value that time at $20 an hour, that is about $16.67 in labor per day. Plug in your own wage and call volume to see your number.

ROAL charges $0.90 per completed phone order, meaning a confirmed order whose ticket reaches the kitchen screen. There is no monthly fee, no setup fee, no per-minute fee, and no contract. Calls, questions, and test calls are free. For owners who want a direct cost comparison, [pricing](/pricing) and [pay per order vs monthly AI phone plans](/compare/monthly-ai-phone-plans) are both worth a look.

sections.h2: How do you set up call forwarding without making a mess?
sections.body:
The cleanest setup is to keep your restaurant number and forward calls to the phone host when you want help. ROAL gives each location its own phone line automatically, and you can forward all calls, or only busy and unanswered calls, depending on your setup.

Forwarding codes vary by carrier and plan, so confirm with your phone company and test with a real call. Common examples are:
- Many landlines and some carriers: dial *72 then the forwarding number to forward all calls, and *73 to turn it off.
- On some GSM mobile carriers: **21*number# forwards all calls, ##21# turns it off, **61*number# forwards unanswered calls, and **67*number# forwards busy calls.
- Verizon Wireless often uses *72 / *73, and *71 for busy/no-answer forwarding.
- Business VoIP systems usually handle forwarding in the web portal.

A simple owner checklist:
1. Decide whether to forward all calls or only no-answer/busy calls.
2. Test one call from a different phone.
3. Confirm the greeting, menu, and hours are right.
4. Make sure staff know where overflow calls land.
5. Turn forwarding off any time you want to go back to normal ringing.

If you want carrier codes in one place, use [call forwarding codes by carrier](/tools/call-forwarding-codes).

sections.h2: What should your staff do when a call needs a person?
sections.body:
Voicemail and phone hosts both have limits. A good restaurant setup sends the weird stuff to staff fast, with enough context to act on it. ROAL hands catering requests, complaints, allergy-sensitive questions, and manager requests to staff with a summary. That means the person taking over does not have to start from zero.

You can write a simple internal rule like this:
- If the caller asks for catering, a refund, an allergy check, or a manager, move it to staff.
- If the caller wants a regular pickup order, let the phone host finish it.
- If the caller says something the host cannot answer, answer it once in the inbox so the host learns it from then on.

That is useful for places with changing specials or tricky menu items. For example, if someone asks, "Is the soup vegetarian today?" and the answer is not in the public menu, staff can update the response once. Then future callers hear the right answer without another voicemail back-and-forth. Owners can also edit hours, FAQs, and menu info from the dashboard.

sections.h2: Which setup fits your restaurant type and rush pattern?
sections.body:
The right answer depends on how your phone behaves during service. A small deli with steady lunch traffic has different needs than a pizza shop on Friday night or a family restaurant that gets many reservation calls.

Use this quick fit table:
| Situation | Voicemail fit | AI phone host fit |
|---|---|---|
| Mostly after-hours calls | Sometimes fine as backup | Very useful for order capture |
| Frequent lunch or dinner rush | Weak fit | Strong fit |
| Many menu questions | Weak fit | Strong fit |
| One-person front counter | Weak fit | Strong fit |
| Lots of manager requests | Backup only | Good with staff handoff |

A practical owner move is to forward only busy or unanswered calls during rush periods, then keep voicemail as the final fallback. That way the restaurant does not lose the chance to take the order live. If you run multiple spots or a busy takeout counter, [multiple locations](/use-cases/multi-location) and [short-staffed shifts](/use-cases/short-staffed) are useful use-case pages to skim.

ROAL is built for restaurants in the U.S., and the first locations were in Jersey City and Hoboken, but the setup works for any U.S. restaurant.

takeaways: Voicemail records a message; an AI phone host can take the order while the caller is on the line.
Use voicemail as backup, not the main path, if you want fewer callbacks and cleaner order flow.
ROAL can answer common questions, take orders, quote ready times, and send tickets to the kitchen screen.
Forwarding should be tested with your carrier before rush hours start.

faq.q: Is voicemail better than an AI phone host for a small restaurant?
faq.a: Voicemail is simpler, but it usually creates more follow-up work. An AI phone host is usually better if you want to take pickup or delivery orders live, answer hours and menu questions, and send a clean ticket to the kitchen. Voicemail is best as a backup when staff are unavailable.

faq.q: Can I use voicemail and an AI phone host together?
faq.a: Yes. Many owners keep voicemail as the last fallback and forward unanswered or busy calls to the phone host first. That gives callers a live answer when possible and still leaves a message path for unusual calls or after-hours overflow.

faq.q: Does ROAL take credit card numbers over the phone?
faq.a: No. ROAL does not take card numbers over the phone. Payment happens at pickup or however your restaurant already takes payment. It can collect the order, name, phone number, modifiers, notes, and ready time.
